You should withdraw
the reference to Kootenay also

All right, I meant to refer to the member for Yale (Mr. Duncan Ross). Where the expenditure runs up into hundreds of thousands of dollars, because these dredging operations run into the millions, the tenderers come down and flaunt themselves before the department, confident that they are going to be able to perpetrate their frauds, and the most wonderful thing is that the government go on dealing with the self same men. When these tenders of the Grant Company were not acted upon by the department, for reasons best known to Mr. Aylesworth, what next happened? Tenders were invited and placed before the department on the 20th May, the former ones having been cancelled immediately. These tenders were invited by telegram, and a number of well known contracting firms either telegraphed or sent down their tenders. There was one from the Wilson Company of Toronto, one from Randolph McNally, one from the Sarnia Company and another from the Goderich Company. They were all willing to tender either by telegram or memo. Mr. Mackay, however, thought something better might be done, and he came right down to the field of operations and placed his tender with the department personally. That is proved by the fact that the envelope bears no postmark in which he placed his tender. Neither did the envelope in which the Grant Company placed their tender bear any postmark. And by a strange coincidence, although these two tenders are for different parts of Midland harbour, Mackay's envelope and Grant's envelope were together, showing how close these contractors are to each other. May I ask where the tenders are for the work to be performed at Victoria harbour?
It must be there.

The Owen Sound Company have a tender in and the Windsor Dredging Company. That is another of

these political associations. It has W. J. McKee at its head, a well known politician. There was another tender put in by this so-called Grant Company afterwards, on the 20th May. 1 am not going to deal with the question of the frauds perpetrated by the unloading of the scows. The evidence given in the committee is so clear that the dishonesty cannot be doubted. Wilkinson, the master of the Mackay dredge, when confronted with the statement which shows that his dredge was employed sixteen hours frankly said that he did not believe the inspector was there, and that the inspector did not know how many scow loads were taken out and whether the scows were full. In the locality it is well known the inspector was not there. I am glad the minister is now taking some precaution by compelling the inspectors to sign a form of declaration. The minister and the Liberal press took great credit from the fact that by refusing to renew the contract and inviting new tenders the country had lost money. What has been the result? In the work at Midland the price paid is 2 cents a yard more. But that is np fault of mine. If the minister thought that the former price was fair, why did he pay a higher price? He could have got the work done at the same rate.
After asking for tenders we let the contract to the lowest.
The minister knew that they had done the work the previous year at 26 cents, and he has himself to blame if anything more was paid.
I do not throw the responsibility of accepting the lowest tender on any one.

If he has succeeded in making the country pay a couple of hundred thousands of dollars more for dredging this year, that is no fault of mine. Parliament voted a certain amount of money for dredging operations ; yet in the face of the direct appropriation by parliament the Mac-kay-Grant Company did work that amounts to $75,000 more than the appropriation, and the minister had to come down with a vote for that amount. Does he propose to do that this year again? Is he going to ask for an appropriation and then let the contractors exceed it to the extent of $75,000 or $100,000? I quite agree that the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway are both doing a large mount of work at Victoria harbour and Clifton and that dredging is required at both these points, but I want to see the country get good value. I do not object to the expenditure ; but when contractors put in tenders which are fraudulent on their face, the department should act with them in a summary manner.
385i

Last year it was found that the approrpiation was exceeded before the close of the season. There was very important work being done by both the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway with a view of getting the harbour ready by the time their railway tracks reached these ports ; and I thought it would be a public misfortune if I were obliged to close down the dredging work before the end of the season. And while, under the contracts, I might have done so, I said they might go on with the work, they taking the risk of the appropriation being made by parliament. I am happy to say that when parliament was asked to make an appropriation in the supplementary estimates of the last fiscal year there was a ready response, no objection being raised. With regard to this year's work, I think that in the supplementary estimates there will be found a sufficient vote to enable the dredges to work during the whole of the present season. It may be that some work will be done beyond the appropriation, but I have reason to believe that the appropriation will be quite sufficient.
Now, with regard to the company with which Mr. Mackay was connected, I do not know why it was that that company did not tender for the work of Tiffin and Midland.

Let me set the minister right at the outset, for I am sure he does not wish to misstate the case. No tenders were called at the commencement of the year for Tiffin. I have the advertisement and the hon. gentleman will see that the dredging was at Midland.

At present, we distinguish between Midland and Tiffin, but we did not at that time. The reason why Tiffin was included in Midland last year was that it forms part of Midland Bay, or even Midland harbour, although the new terminals of the railway company are being made in a very different place from the terminals at Midland. Now, my hon. friend, I think, would have achieved great eminence if he had adopted a different profession. His abilities, certainly, would have adorned the profession which was mane famous by the celebrated Sherlock Holmes. Even in the matter of the comparison of handwriting, my hon. friend is able to see with absolute certainty resemblances in the handwriting of different documents which nobody else is able to discover. Take the tenders for Penetanguishene and Owen Sound and my hon. friend can see resemblances in the figures written in these two tenders, which, I am positive, no other hon, member of this House or anybody else will be able to see. I have looked at the two, and while I admit that there is some

resemblance In tbe handwriting in some parts, yet in the figures, which are the essential thing to show collusion, there is not the slightest resemblance. Yet the hon. gentleman is able to say without a moment's hesitation that they were written by the same hand.
Is there any resemblance in the handwriting?

I said that in some parts there was some resemblance. But I have had a large experience in court and my experience tells me that if a man has a vivid imagination he can see resemblances in handwriting specimens that one less gifted would fail to discover. When experts in handwriting desire to find resemblances, it seems the easiest thing in the world for them to do so. The result of my experience is that I do not place great reliance on the tests of experts in handwriting. With regard to the figures which, as I have said, are the crucial thing, I venture to say that the figures in the two tenders do not bear the slightest resemblance, nor is there anything else to indicate that they were prepared by the same person. Now, when these tenders came to the attention of the minister he found that there were three tenders, one from the Owen Sound Company, one from the Penetanguishene Company, and one from the Dominion Dredging Company, the prices being 57 cents, 53 cents and 30 cents. It was obviously the minister's duty to accept the lowest tender. He accepted the Dominion Dredging Company's tender, and advised the company of that fact. They had tendered for other works on the St. Lawrence and other rivers; and they informed the minister that with the other contracts which they had accepted and the work they had to do, they would not be able to perform this work, not having a sufficient dredging plant. And so they declined to do the work at 30 cents. What better evidence does the hon. gentleman want that there is nothing in his statement-which, if not unparliamentary, I would call a reckless statement-that it is the practice of these companies to combine and secure whatever prices they desire from the government, than the fact that the Dominion Dredging Company which he likes to call the ' Stewart Company,' because Mr. Stewart happens to be the son of a member of this House-what better evidence could he desire of the lack of foundation of his statement than the fact that when the Dominion Dredging Company could not do the work, and, in a perfectly proper manner the minister called for new tenders, the company with which Mr. Mae-kay is connected, which, for some reason that I am not aware of, probably a perfectly good reason had not tendered before, tendered for 27 cents a cubic yard? So the country got the work done at 3 cents Mr. PUGSLEY.
a cubic yard less than the lowest tender, that of the Dominion Dredging Company, which he has so frequently mentioned in this House in terms, certainly, not of the greatest respect. Can any fault be found with the minister?
Six o'clock.
I would suggest that this item be passed-
No, no.

Then, I shall have some remarks to make after recess.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Just betore recess I was making some observations in reply to my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Bennett). I shall not pursue the matter along the same lines beyond saying this, for I want to be as brief as possible. My hon. friend has failed to point out that in any single case the department has accepted any other but the lowest tender; in every case the contract for dredging work has been given to the lowest tenderer. There have been a few cases, very few indeed, in which there has been a failure to perform the contract satisfactorily on the part of certain companies, in these cases the contracts have been given to the next lowest tenderer, provided he has brought his price down to the price of the lowest tenderer. But with those exceptions, which have occurred very rarely the contract has always been awarded by competition to the lowest tenderer. I may also say that in some cases where the work is urgent, exceptions have been made, in cases where it was necessary that work should be done immediately.
Now my hon. friend referred to the fact that something had been said in the newspapers regarding the objection which he made to the extension of the dredging contracts. I do not know what has been said, but il do know that after the matter had been raised in the House by the hon. gentleman, when I decided to extend the dredging contracts, there were in the newspapers supporting hon. gentlemen opposite, strong expressions of triumph at what was supposed to be some great act performed in the jrublic interest and which would redound to the party benefit. Now I want to say a word or two with regard to the extension of the dredging contracts. When the question of how to deal with the various dredging works came before us, I looked into the existing contracts, looked into the prices, and I found they provided that the dredging should be completed during the then current season, or at such other date as might be fixed by the minister. It seemed very

clear that under the terms of the contracts,
I had power, if I thought it in the public interest so to do, to fix a later date for the completion of the work. I asked for a report from the chief engineer of my department with reference to the prices which were being paid for the various dredging work that was being done under the different contracts. His report was that in all cases the prices were fair and reasonable. In many cases they seemed to me very low, and I am free to say to the committee that I thought that it would unquestionably be in the public interest if I could extend those contracts and give until the end of the present year for their completion, where that time was necessary in order to complete them. But the hon. gentleman voicing the sentiments of the opposition raised an objection to that. Well, I felt that the views of the opposition were entitled to respect. They represent a large and important section of the people of this country, although numerically a considerable minority of the people. Still, they represent an important section, and their opinions are entitled to respect. I felt that if there could be any ground of criticism levelled against me and levelled against those with whom I have the honour to be associated, not only my colleagues in the government but our supporters in this House and throughout this country-I felt that I ought not to subject them "to that criticism. So in looking into the matter more closely, I found that the advertisements for tender's which were issued last year called for dredging during the then present season. My hon. friend had not called the attention of the committee, and had not called my attention to that. But in consequence of the matter poming up, and as I felt that if there were any ground of criticism it was my duty to remove it, I looked back to see what were the advertisements which called for tenders on which these contracts had been let, and finding that the advertisements were limited in the way I have mentioned, I came to the conclusion that, even although the contracts upon their face gave me power to fix a later date for the completion of the work, yet upon the whole there might be a question as to whether the contracts were not broader than was warranted by the advertisements. In view, therefore, of the objection which was raised by the opposition, and in view of the criticism which I knew would be levelled against me and against the government if I were to extendi the contracts, I thought it would be better for me to yield to the objection which had been raised, and to issue an advertisement for new tenders I did so, Mr. Chairman, and 1 did so reluctantly, because I felt that the extension of the contracts would be in the public interest. I felt it would be a saving of money to the country to extend the contracts. However, as I say, I yielded to the
objection which had been made, and in view of the circumstances regarding the advertisements for tenders. Well, the result of calling for new tenders has been that in the great majority of cases, although the widest possible publicity was given to the advertisements, and although in many cases a large number of tenders were received, the total result has been that the price at which the lowest tenderer in each case tendered, is, with few exceptions, considerably higher er than the price at which the work was being done last year. I will give some examples. In the case of Owen Sound, the contract was being done last year for materials, outside of rock, at 20 cents per cubic yard; the lowest tender this year was 25 cents per cubic yard.
Who is the tenderer ?

Mr. Bowman. And Mr. Boone also tendered. Mr. Boone's tender was 28 cents per cubic yard, 8 cent's higher than the price given last year. The lowest tenderer this year was 5 cents per cubic yard higher than the price last year. In the case of the Hamilton work it was done last year at 12 cents per cubic yard, the lowest tender this year is 15 cents.
Who is the tenderer?

Mr. Phinn. Mr. Healey, the next tenderer, 23 cents. At Cobourg there were five tenderers: Phinn at 18 cents, Morgan at 22 cents, Healy at 23, Randolph & Macdonald at 23, and Manley at 30. Last year the work was being done at the low price of 11 cents per cubic yard, 7 cents per cubic yard lower than the lowest tender of this year, and 19 cents per cubic yard lower than the highest tender of this year. In that case there were five tenderers for the work. In the case of Goderich there were three tenderers : Horton at 35 cents, Manley & Co. at 35 cents, and J. B. Bertram, of Toronto, at 42 cents. Mr. Bertram is a dredging contractor. He is doing work at Port Burwell at present. The price of_the work last year, 25 cents per cubic yard7 was one cent per cubic yard less than the lowest tender this year and 17 cents lower than the highest of this year. In the case of Midland this year there was only one tender at 28 cents, while last year it was 26 cents, a difference of 2 cents. The Canadian Dredging and Construction Company has the contract. At Little Current the price this year is a little less than last year. Last year it was 30 cents and this year it is 25 cents. The same contractor, Mr. Boone, has the work.
How many tenders were there at Little Current?
Two.
Who was the second ?
Mr. Bowman. At Wingfield basin, Boone tendered last year and
Who had it last year?

Prendergast, of Montreal. He lost a great deal of money on it. In Toronto last year the work was being done at 13J cents, but this year it is 19i cents. The work is being done by Healy who is the only tenderer. At Penetang, Bowman who had it last year at 14 cents was the only tenderer this year at 19 cents.
Did the minister of his own accord raise the dredging there from 14 cents to 19J cents?

Not of my own accord. We advertised publicly for tenders and the lowest tender was 19 cents. It was a question of accepting that tender or not proceeding with the work. My hon. friend seems to think it would be a proper thing for the minister when he advertised publicly for tenders for dredging work and did not get any which according to the judgment of the chief engineer were reasonable,
* to refuse to accept tenders and not go on with the work.
Did the chief engineer certify when the price was 14 cents that it was reasonable and also when it was 19 cents?

Yes, and my chief engineer was of opinion and so advised me that in a large number of these contracts last year the work was being done not only at a reasonable price, but at a lower price than we could ever expect to get contractors to tender for the work at.
Rot.
Another remarkable instance was at Port Burweli, where there were four tenders this year. Bertram and Company tendered at 39 cents, Finn at 43
cents, Horton at 44 cents and Manley at 45 cents, all most reliable contractors, men of large experience and of the highest reputation.
Horton included ?
Horton included.
You should read the evidence in the East Elgin trial to a man of that name who took part in marking ballots.
I feel very sorry that my hon. friend has this unfortunate disposition to find fault.
I say truthful things about men of the stamp of Horton whose reputation is known in Ontario.

I cannot help thinking that when my hon. friend retires from the House and gets home in the silence of his bedroom he must regret the disagreeable things he has said because there is no lasting pleasure in that sort of thing.
The minister may hear some things of himself if he does not keep a little bridle on his unruly tongue.

I have heard a great many things about myself and very nasty things in my lifetime, and there is no man living who can say anything against me that I should be ashamed or afraid to hear, no man living.
I was explaining that at Port Burweli there were four tenders, and the lowest tender this year was 39 cents, while last year the work was done at 15J cents. Our information is that the contractor was losing money upon that contract last year. I need not go through all the others, but I will take the case of the Thames. There there were four tenders, the Bertram Company at 24 cents, Horton at 22 cents Healy at 23 cents and Manley at 20 cents. Last year that work was done at 13 cents.
The total result, as near as I am able to figure it out, taking in Ontario and Quebec, of the calling for new tenders-and I regret that this should be the case-has been to cost the Dominion somewhere between $175,000 and $200,000 more than it would have if I had extended the contracts and insisted on the work going on at the same price as that in force last year.
Why did you not extend it?

I have already explained the reason. I take, of course, the full responsibility, but I have been obliged to assume that responsibility under the circumstances I have mentioned. I felt as I have said, that the contracts gave me full power to extend them, and I felt in view of the low price at which the work was being done that it would have been the part of wisdom for my hon. friend who has been
JULY 6, ia08
commissioned by our hon. friends opposite to take charge of the criticism of dredging contracts and who speaks for the opposition, to have acquiesced in what I proposed to do, but, as I said, under the circumstances that it was due to myself and to the government and to the friends supporting us to ask for new tenders and then, having called for new tenders, I felt that as the prices were certified to be reasonable by the chief engineer it was my duty to accept the lowest tenders.

The minister finds fault with the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) for complaining because tenders were not advertised for in the usual way during the present year and he tries to show that the country has lost money by having to pay larger prices than what were paid last year. If these contractors were willing to do this work at the same prices that they were paid last year, it reflects seriously on the hon. minister that he gave them a renewal of the contract at the advanced prices he has stated.
I did not renew a single contract. I asked for public tenders, and gave the contract to the lowest tenderer.

And they are going to 'be paid $175,000 more this year than they were paid last year for the same work. 1 would think that the hon. minister, when he received a tender of 26 cents for work that was done last year for 14 cents per cubic yard, while the contractor was willing to do it this year at the same price, would have hesitated before making a contract at nearly double the price paid before. We learned in the Public Accounts Committee that on all these dredging works the government appointed as inspectors men Who had really never had any experience in dredging work.
All of them ?
Nearly all of them. I defy the hon. member to name one who had any previous experience of dredging work.
The man at Penetang sail), he had been doing it for three years.

What was he before 'he went into the dredging business ? One inspector swore that the engineer in charge, I think Mr. Sing from Toronto, only visited the works once or twice during the whole season. This same inspector had charge of two dredges, and he farmed out one part of the work to another man. Any one can see at a glance that in that way the government must necessarily lose. The contractors have everything in their own hands. The chief engineer of the Public Works'De-partment and all of the staff will swear that the only honest way to pay for this work Is by scow measurement ; and yet these inspectors swear that they cannot come within from ten to thirty yards of the actual
measurement in a scow. On the other hand, the Department of Railways and Canals will tell you that to pay by scow measurement is almost sure to result in a loss to the government, and in their contracts they specify that the work must be measured in situ. The officers of the government swore that the scow measurement made a difference of about one-third.

It was stated that the price given per cubic yard in situ is always different from the price by scow measurement. It is understood that there is an expansion of from 30 to 40 per cent, which is always figured on.
There is no doubt there is an expansion. By the scow measurement there is no way of telling whether you get the right quantity or not. The scow may or may not be filled.	.
The scows are filled.
How can the minister say that when the inspectors admitted that they did not see all the scows going out ?
In the great majority of cases they did. All the inspectors swore that.
It is the duty of the inspector to see every scow that goes out, and in the forms that I have prescribed he must swear that he was personally present and saw every scow go out.

I admit that that is his duty, but he has not been doing it. I believe the government has not been getting the actual measurement in a single contract by this scow measurement. That is the reason I find fault with this method of paying the contractors. When any dredging is to be done, a profile of the work is made before it is commenced, so that the government know exactly the quantity of stuff 'to be dredged out when it is in situ ; but With the scow' measurement, there is no check at all, especially with the kind of inspectors the government have been employing on these works. I claim that on every dredging contract work involving hundreds of thousands of dollars, there should be an engineer. But we have an engineer located in Toronto, and perhaps a tailor or a shoe-inaker acting as an inspector of the work, and not even keeping track of the number of scow's that go out.
Will the hon. member tell me what the inspector's duties are on the scow ?
According to the minister, his duty is to tell the quantity of material in each scow as it goes away from the dredge.
Could not a shoemaker tell w'hether a scow was full or not ?

He might possibly, but 1 should think he would be better engaged in making shoes. What I claim is that there should be an engineer stationed on 'the work to see that the contract is properly carried out; and he should have an assistant under him capable of estimating the quantity of material in the scow.
Tile inspector is not to estimate the quantity in the scow. The contents of the scow are given him by the engineer, and it is his duty to see that no scow goes out unless it is filled.
If that is the case, the hon. minister, if he was at the Public Accounts Committee, knows that hundreds of scows went out only half filled.
And the inspector swore that when they were only half filled he charged them as being only half filled.
When a scow was only half filled, the inspector, who never had any experience in measuring scows, stated that 'he had simply to guess the quantity in the scow.
Was not that' an exceptional case, in which, owing to low water, the scow could not go out fully loaded ?
I challenge the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) to produce a return in which it was sworn that there was less than the full amount in the scow.

The inspector swore that half sco'ws went out. The hon. member for East Simcoe asked how it was that full scow loads were charged. He said that the two halves were added together, and he made his return accordingly.

There was a case, as the minister stated, in which a scow went out only partially loaded on account of the low water. But in every contract it is left solely and entirely to the inspector to estimate the quantity the government are paying for. I claim that if the Public Works Department are going to continue this dredging work by contract, they should have an engineer on each work every day. It is not in the interest of the public or in the interest of the Public Works Department or in the interest of the minister, to let a large dredging contract involving hundreds of thousands of dollars, and to leave it entirely to the kind of men the government have been appointing as inspectors to decide the amount the government has to pay under these contracts.
Would the hon. gentleman advocate the policy of having a civil engineer continuously on every dredging job ?
The amount the government is paying engineers in charge of these

works is, I think, not more than $150 a' month, and the inspectors receive something like $3 a day. I would ask the hon. member for Lambton,i if he had a work involving the expenditure of several hundreds of thousands of dollars, whether as a business man he would not pay the difference and have an experienced engineer qualified to measure the work and go into it thoroughly and know exactly the quantity in each scow ?

AH I can say in answer to my hon. friend's question is that throughout the whole investigation in the Public Accounts Committee this year into the dredging contracts, it has not been shown by any evidence that any inspector made any false return, or that the country was injured in the very least. If it was shown that the returns were honestly made, why add to the expense, when hon. gentlemen opposite are always complaining of the expenses of the government ?
I am surprised at the hon. gentleman making the statement that it has not been shown that the government have lost anything. He knows that one inspector inspected for two dredges.

It was not shown that anything was lost. It was shown that one inspector had been guilty of malfeasance in office by farming out his job, but the moment the government found that out he was dismissed. But it was not shown that the returns were untrue.
How could we show anything else ?
Why draw a conclusion if there is no evidence from which to draw it ?
We had the evidence of the government engineers that the scows varied to the extent of from ten to twenty yards.
And you have the further evidence that just what was in the scow was returned.

I would like to call the attention of the committee to the point raised by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) at the beginning of the discussion on this question, which the minister has not yet elucidated; that is, the resemblance of the handwriting in two rival tenders for this dredging work at Midland and Waubaushene. The hon. member for East Simcoe asked me to have a look into the handwriting of these two tenders, and I have done so, and there is no doubt that the addresses on the two envelopes are in the same handwriting.
Has the hon. gentleman looked at the figures setting down the prices?

I will come to those in a moment. There is no doubt that both ten-

ders are addressed in the same handwriting-
Neither of which was accepted by the minister.
That does not matter.

I have not followed the discussion enough to draw conclusions ; I am only pointing out the fact. The minister states that the tenders are in different handwriting ; but, strange to say, if you compare the body of the writing in the Grant company tender for Midland harbour with the body of the writing in the Spohn company tender for the same work, it is exactly the same ; so that although there is something in the contention of the minister that in the two first tenders, which are presumably rival tenders, there is some difference in the body of the tenders though none in the addresses, still if you take another pair of tenders and compare the Grant tender with the Spohn tender, you find them in exactly the same handwriting, -whatever conclusion you may draw from the fact. I would like to say, with reference to the dredging in the province of Quebec, that it is considered the greatest windfall possible to obtain a dredging contract from the government. There has been a regular scramble for them for years, and you find people who have had no experience at all going into the dredging business. Those who have been successful in obtain ing such contracts in the province of Quebec live very well. I know these men. They were in rather penurious circumstances before they went into this business, but now they dazzle us with the luxury of their living. Some are lawyers. My hon. friend mentioned Mr. Morgan. Mr. Morgan has gone into the dredging business and I remember when Mr. Morgan was practising law.
Has he made a fortune out of It?
It is very difficult to say of any man that he has made a fortune, but the indications are that he found the dredging business more profitable than the ^practice of law.
It cannot be contended that Mr. Morgan is a political friend of the government.

He is a very strong political friend, a friend of the deepest dye. He is like many so called Conservatives, who have cleaved to the present government, ready to support it under any circumstances.
'Mr. UBMIEUX. I know personally that Mr. Morgan was three times the Conservative candidate in the county of .Richelieu.

And I remember a very hotly contested campaign we had in the city of Montreal in which Mr. Prefontaine.
a friend of the Postmaster General, was a candidate, and in that contest the Conservative Mr. Morgan was working for him for all he was worth. At that time Mr. Morgan had gone into the dredging business. I am speaking of facts that are admitted. In the province of Quebec when you find a man suddenly prosperous, you ask: has he got a dredging contract? It is notorious. We have Mr. Prendergast.
Has he made a fortune?
I do not know, but he lives well-much better than people who work harder.
Mr. Frendergast will tell you that there is not much money in dredging unless you have considerable experience.

They all say that, but the facts are there. They all seem to prosper. And outside of lawyers, whose occupation and technical knowledge would not lead them to dredging, there are coal merchants. It is extraordinary how coal merchants go in for dredging. In the province of Quebec we have Mr. Cowan and Moore & Company. My hon. friend the Postmaster General knows these people. They are coal merchants and they have found it advantageous to leave their occupation and go in for dredging; and although they always pretend there is nothing in it, they still tender and try to obtain the work, and having obtained it they seem to thrive considerably on the profits. As a rule-and I assert this on my responsibility as a member-the dredging is pooled in the province of Quebec. Tenders are sent in and it looks very regular, but when the work comes to be divided, some find they cannot attend to it here and others that they cannot attend to it there, and as a matter of fact the contract is divided up among them so that each is satisfied. We should abandon that old system of giving out dredging in order to distribute patronage, and have a policy dictated by the urgency of solving our transportation problem.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to have my hon. friend's approval. I expected when he came into office that he would find somewhere, wherever it is to be found-I had a great deal of difficulty in finding it in the Department of Public Works-the valuable report of the transportation commission, and that he would see if it was not possible to put into execution the suggestion so well and so urgently made by that commission, and cast aside this system of doing odd-jobs here and there just to please political friends. Go to the province of Quebec, and you will find dredging done in the most impossible places at the greatest expense. It is a race among the friends of the gov-

ernment as to who will have the most influence and get dredging done in his county. Whether the dredging is really necessary is a matter of very secondary importance. Whether it will enter into the scheme of transportation, is not considered at all. The only thing thought of is who can exert the greatest influence to have it done in his own county. You will find one place in the St. Lawrence where last year the government spent between $28,000 and $30,000 dredging a channel across the river, through the soil under the river, and on account of the current the channel fills up as quickly as it is dredged. Ask the people on either side: What about this channel that is being dredged? They smile and they will tell you it is being dredged, but it fills up just as fast again. Everybody knows that a channel across the St. Lawrence in the vicinity of Lake St. Peter, where the soil is extremely soft, must fill up at once, but the government will go on dredging there as long as people have influence to get it done.
Will my hon. friend state where that is?

No, but I will tell it privately to my hon. friend. I do not want my criticism to be taken down into that county and be tortured into an opposition by me to public works in the province of Quebec. But I would be glad to inform the minister privately of the circumstances connected with that political piece of waste and extravagance.

I am sincerely desirous of finding out whether any work is going on which is not required in the public interest. If I can find any evidence of that, I will stop the work. WThen my hon. friend refers to an important matter like that, done in the channel of the St. Lawrence, he ought not to have the slightest objection to making it known.
(Mr. MONK. No objection whatever, and I will give my hon. friend the information with pleasure. In other parts of the country, you will find dredging done in small rivers, where there is really no call for it. You will find dredging done around some island belonging to an influential proprietor, in order to make his island larger, and fill up the space around it. You will find dredging done at considerable cost to the country in order to facilitate the approach to the private ice house of an ice dealer in a favoured locality.
Where is that being done ?

I shall give the information with pleasure, and my hon. friend can verify it. You find dredging done in these localities by these contractors who are on the most friendly basis with the sitting Mr. MONK.
member, who have obtained the contracts for them. They make the sitting member presents and treat him well and they are always together. I mention these facts- why? Because if my hon. friend is sincere, if we are to go back to the suggestions of the transportation commission, there is most important dredging to be done which cannot wait, if we are going to compete with our neighbours to the south. It is often alleged that we have a thirty foot channel from Montreal to Quebec. A thirty foot channel is one of the improvements most impressed on the government by the transportation commission. If we are going to solve the problem of transportation from Montreal to the sea, the commissioners consider it very important that we should at once have a thirty-foot channel. I have heard it alleged by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that we have that at present. I doubt that statement. I do not say that it was not made candidly, but from what information I have gained from experienced men, pilots and others interested in shipping, there are several points between Montreal and Quebec where it is by no means certain that we have that depth at low water. Therefore, I say that, with the increasing size of ships, it is most necessary for us to carry out the suggestions, and, if we have dredging to do, it must not be done to advance private interests, it must be done at the points where it is so urgently needed, there are two points between Montreal and Quebec where the channel is very narrow, as is pointed out in the report of the commission. Large ships sailing through these parts of the river, even if a fog supervenes, cannot cast anchor, for, if they do that, the ship will turn and there is no room to allow it to turn in safety. Consequently they must go on and trust to luck and the signals. And accidents have occurred there on-that account. It seems to me that the suggestions of the Transportation Commission ought to be heeded first and foremost. Why? Because the rates of insurance are against us as compared with those of American ports, and this is precisely on account of the difficulties which, I say, we can eliminate promptly if we reserve for these expenditures the money which we spend uselessly elsewhere.
In the same way, if my hon. friend will take the trouble to ascertain, he will find out that we are paying a great deal for dredging in the Ottawa river, which, I think, could be done in a better way if we keep in mind that the Georgian Bay canal has been investigated and recommended as a work of national importance, and dredge where it will be useful for that channel, instead of dredging to suit the convenience of political favourites and members of parliament who do not take the trouble to investigate these large ques-

tions, but are satisfied simply to have the work done in their own counties.
Where is dredging done ot that kind?

I mentioned a moment ago that, to my knowledge, dredging was done in the Ottawa river, last summer or the summer before, to facilitate the approach to a private ice-house. That is somewhere in the county of Vaudreuil. If my hon. friend will take the trouble to investigate he will find that that is absolutely correct.
Peterborough steamboat landing, $$2,500.

That may be dropped.
Mr. 8AM. HUGHES. Why?

Because the work has been completed and paid for.
Petewawa-extension of wharf, $11,500.
Of that $8,500 is a revote. We have added $3,000 more on further investigation, because of the larger amount of cribwork which must be built.
Has the contract been let?
No.
Is it to be put up by public tender?
If built, it will be by public tender. I am not absolutely sure as to whether I will go on with that work at the present time or not. I am looking into the question of the public necessity for it.
While we are on the subject of wharfs, I would ask the minister the nature of the report made by the engineer of his department sent to inspect a wharf at Brighton.

I am under the impression that I gave the hon. gentleman (Mr. Owen) that information. We have not had a report yet. There was a report some years ago. Owing to my having received information that the owner of the wharf declined to sell, I have taken no further proceedings.
The hon. minister will remember that the chief engineer, Mr. Glass, was down there a few weeks before the deputation came to Ottawa.
There is no Mr. Glass an engineer in my department.
If an engineer was sent from the Department of Public Works to Brighton, will the minister bring down a report to the committee at some future meeting?
Certainly.
Which department would have charge of this wharf-Public Works or Railways?

This is a private wharf.
(Mr. OWEN. There are two private wharfs there, and both are in a dilapidated condition. Brighton is a thriving town of 1,800 people, yet the wharf there is a disgrace to the Dominion of Canada. Some months ago a deputation came down and the minister was going to do something, for it was clearly suown then that something was needed. I hope he is not going to wait until the general election.

My hon. friend will remember that a delegation waited upon me. and I think he accompanied that delegation. It was stated that there was a private wharf which it was desirable the department should purchase, making the necessary repairs, and make it a public wharf. I said I was not prepared to undertake the expropriation of a private wharf at Brighton at present, but if they could obtain from the owner a statement that he was willing to sell at what was regarded as a reasonable price, I would take the matter into consideration. Some little time afterwards I received word from one of the most prominent members of the delegation-
What name?
I have forgotten the name-that the owner of the wharf refused to put a price on it. So I have done nothing further in the matter.

I would like to know 'if the Department of Public Works had an engineer there at all. The member for East Northumberland (Mr. Owen) says that the government sent an engineer to look over the wharf, and the Minister of Public Works said they did not.
The chief engineer informs me that he has given no instructions to any engineer of the department to make an examination.

I am surprised to hear the Minister of Public Works say that he does not know- that there is a necessity for this work in connection with the Petawawa wharf. Last session I brought the matter to the attention of the acting Minister of 'Public Works, and an appropriation was made in the supplementaries. During the summer I took the matter up with the department, and they assured me that the w'ork would be commenced last August, 'but up to the present time nothing has been done. I have here a letter from the manager of the Pembroke Navigation Company which I would like to read to the House :
Dear Sir,-Some time ago I brought to your attention the matter of the extension of the Petewawa wharf. At that time I pointed out the urgent necessity of the carrying out of this work. I understand that there was an amount in the estimates passed last session ' for this purpose. Up to the present nothing

has been done although you informed me that according to a conversation you had with the engineer of the Public Works Department, this work would have been commenced last August. As you are aware during the low water season, we are unable to land our boats there without danger of going on the shoals or reefs which are in close proximity to the dock in its present condition. We have also had trouble with the government booms swinging out beyond the end of the wharf and blocking the channel so that we were prevented from landing. I trust you will bring this matter to the attention of the government and endeavour to have the work completed at the earliest moment possible as this is an iin-portant point for landing supplies and men for the military camp, the settlers and the lumbering interests on the Petewawa river.
Yours truly,
GEORGE SCHMIDT, Manager and Secretary Treasurer.
I would like to impress upon the minister the necessity of undertaking this work as soon as possible. During the season of low water it is almost impossible to get up to this dock with boats. It is a very important point on the Ottawa river at the present time.

Of course, nothing could be done until parliament voted the money. We are getting along pretty late in the season and not much can be done this year. 'But my attention has been called to the wharf at Petawawa, and it has been intimated to me that the wharf really is not necessary in the public interest. I have directed an inquiry to be made, and I can say to my hon. friend that the matter is still under consideration.
The wharf in its present condition is practically useless at low water.

It is not positively decided that this large amount of money will be expended there. I am not sure it is iu the public interest.
I>ort Burwell-improvement to harbour, $90,000.

Up to the 31st of December there was $S,769 expended. Then there was an estimate for a further expenditure up the 31st of March. The dredging work is under contract.
Port Hope-repairs to pier and dredging, $15,000.
What has been done at Port Hope this year ?
We propose to, do some dredging at Port Hope. It was commenced In the fall of 1907, by Mr. Phin of Welland. We hope to do quite a little dredging work this year.
Will there be any repairs 'to the piers ?
Yes, we propose to make repairs to the pier, also to do some dredging.

Port Stanley-harbour improvements, $38,-
000.
Is this all for the outside breakwater in Port Stanley ?
This is for the outside breakwater, and for dredging. The work is under contract.
When will that work for the outside breakwater be completed 1
I think it will take another year.
Who is the inspector ?
My memorandum does not say, hut I can get the name.

I know the inspector has been changed, and I wanted to know tile reason. I wrote the minister in connection with the inside breakwater six weeks or two months ago. I called his attention to the condition of the inside breakwater on the east side of the east pier. Unless that breakwater is extended 150 feet to the northeast, practically the work that has been done in Port Stanley will be useless. The lake is breaking in on the north side of the breakwater, and is cutting into the harbour.

I will have the matter looked into at once.
Rainy river-improvements at Long Sault rapids, $501,000.

In reference to that, we were obliged to get the consent of the United States government, because it might be a matter for the Waterways Commission to settle. At their suggestion wh have referred the matter to the American government.
In connection with a similar matter, is any expenditure being incurred by the department in keeping a patrol tug or tugs at a point called the Lime Kilns, near Windsor ?

My engineer tells nre no.
Roche's point wharf, $3,200.
What is that dock costing at Roche's Point ?
The total cost is $3,212. That has been paid for.
I understand the people In that vicinity never wanted that wharf, and they are now asking the government to take it away.

Well, they have not tome to the right source to get it done, because they have not communicated with me bn the subject.

* Mr. J. D. REID. Was there not some 'complaint about this wharf not being re-jquired ?

The chief engineer says 'there has been some complaint, but it has 'not come to my notice.
' Mr. J. D. REID. The wharf was never 'required, the people petitioned against the 'wharf being built, it was forced on them 'and now they want it taken away.

I was mistaken. I saw the chief engineer bow his head when you were speaking, but he says there has been no complaint to the department in regard to the work not being necessary.
Rondeau harbour-improvements, $50,000.

The total probable cost of the works is about $130,000. The works consist of the construction of two breakwaters each 500 feet long, dredging of the site of the breakwaters to a depth of 23 feet, dredging and approach to the depth of 22 feet, dredging the turning basin in the inner harbour, repairs to piers, &c. The dredging is under contract to the Canadian Construction and Dredging Company whose headquarters are at Toronto. I think Mr. Bertram is president or manager.
Rossport-wharf on north shore Lake Superior, $5,000.

This is a coal dock or wharf in connection with the Canadian Pacific. It is in Thunder Bay and Rainy River district.
Sault Ste Marie wharf-dredging approaches, $30,000.

The dredging contract has been given to the Great Lakes Dredging Company.
Severn river-improvement of waterway at McDonald's chute No. 1, $1,000.
This may be dropped.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Item dropped.
Southampton-repairs to Chantry island breakwater, $3,500.

This will finish the work. It is by day labour.
Toronto harbour improvements, $90,000.
This is a revote.
Is it under contract?

The dredging is under contract to the Western Dredging Company and the protection work is also under contract.
Victoria harbour-improvements, $56,200.
Prior to 31st March, 1908, we expended here $10,331.33. We contemplated much more work this year. This is under contract to the Canadian Dredging and Contracting Company.
Reverting to the item of which I spoke I have found the newspaper clipping. It says :

Sing, chief engineer, from the Public Works, Toronto, and Frank L. Wood, Liberal candidate for the House of Commons for East Northumberland, were here (Brighton) on Tuesday when the chief engineer made an inspection of the wharf for the purpose of making a report to the government as to the advisability of taking over the same. Our wharf should be repaired and extended, and we sincerely hope the government will grant the prayer of the large petition recently presented to them.
I asked the minister the contents of that report. This is dated May 27. I gave the name of Glass instead of Sing in speaking before.

Mr. Sing is the resident engineer in Toronto. I have no doubt he has made an inspection of the wharf, pro, bably when visiting at Colborne, but I will take occasion to see if there is a report from him and if not to get the result of his examination.
Did Mr. Sing go there on instructions from the department or on his own responsibility?
I will have the files /ooked up to ascertain.
Surely the chief engineer will understand something of the matter?	"

The chief engineer says he has no recollection of sending Mr. Sing tnere.
Winnipeg river-improvements, $10,000,
What is the nature of these improvements?
These are at Miller's rapids, north of ICenora, and Throat rapids to improve a stretch of navigation of 16 miles to the crossing of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.
I wish for some information about the wharf which is to cost $13,000 on Lake Frangois in the county of Beauce.
What does my hon. friend want to know?

I will give the minister some information, because he is new in his office and I don't think I should blame everything on him for that reason. There was money voted two years ago for a wharf there and the wharf was built, and like the other public works throughout the country I presume it was left to the member for the county to look after the building of it. I do not know whether the government sent an engineer there or not, but if they did they might as well send an old grandmother. Do you hear that,

Mr. Minister? Your engineers do not amount to a row of pins. Here is an example where the engineer recommended a wharf to be built and the wharf was built, and there was no stone put Into it,, and away went the wharf with the ice last' spring. Now, this is a small lake, about twenty-five miles long by two or three miles wide, and there is no current in it.
Are there any boats on the lake?

Yes, but they belong to the lumber company and the lumber company uses its own wharf. There was $7,000 wasted on this wharf before, and I would like the minister to explain why he wants to waste $13,000 more now.

I think my hon. friend is in error with regard to the importance of the matter, because my information is there was a large petition in favour of this work, and upon investigation it was decided to be in the public interest to build the wharf. It would appear there are several steamboats plying on the lake.
There are, but they belong to the lumber company, and they use their own wharf.

I am glad to get the information from my hon. friend in regard to the alleged defects in the wharf, and I will have the matter looked into. The work is under contract, and the contractor will have to complete the work properly before he is paid.
Who is the contractor?
John Lowry, of Ottawa.

How long is the wharf to
be?
The Lambton wharf will have a total length of 350 feet extending out to 6 feet at low water. The Coleraine wharf will have a total length of 300 feet.
The minister says there are boats plying on that lake ; where do they start from and where do they go to?
I am sorry to say I do not know.
I believe you know very well.

This is another ease where the member for the county apparently got up a petition and the government immediately proceeded to spend thousands of dollars on a wharf without inquiring whether it was necessary or not. The facts stated by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin) prove that this money is squandered for political purposes.

I can tell the minister that I will get no thanks for what I have said Mr. MORIN
in the House to-night. Well, I want none. Every time I condemn unnecessary expenditure here, next day the Grits on the other side go for me, and say : Why did you say anything against that work being
uie in the province Quebec ; Ontario gets so much and the other provinces get so much, and we want to get our share. Well, the government is just squandering the money, and it would seem that all the Liberal member for a county needs to do is to ask for an expenditure, whether it is necessary or not, and he gets it. That was the policy of the previous Minister of Public Works ; I don't accuse the present minister, because he is new in the office, and I shall not hang him before giving him a trial. I have here estimates for the last seven years, and what do they show? Every year there is expenditure in the Island of Orleans, at St. Frangois, at St. Laurent and Ste. Famille. At St. Frangois the population is about 500 ; it is situated at the lower end of the island, and they have a wharf there and another one about half a mile distant. At St. Jean de Orleans and St. Laurent it is the same thing. The thing is getting ridiculous. The member for the county asks for the money and he gets it, right or wrong. Is that what Sir Wilfrid Laurier promised before he came to power? In my county, in 1895, he told the people that if he came to power his government would be a government of example. He just omitted that little word ' bad,' for since he has come to power his government has been a government of bad example. He found fault with the Conservatives spending $36,000,000 a year, but immediately on his coming to power in 1896 we voted $52,000,000 at the special session of that year ; the next year the estimates were $58,000,000, the next year $62,000,000, the next year $70,000,000, the next year $78,000,000, the next year $82,000,000, the next year $105,000,000 and this year we have $119,000,000 in the main estimates and $9,000,000 more in supplementaries already brought down, and the minister tells us there are more to come, and God only knows how many supplementary estimates he will have. The man who found fault with the late government for spending $35,000,000 or $40,000,000 is going to spend this year $140,000,000 or $150,000,000. What does that look like?
It looks good to me.

But you are a Grit like the rest.
Manitoba-Grand Marais harbour, Lake Winnipeg-improvement of entrance, $1,500.
What is the nature of this work ?
It is to remove the sandbar to improve the entrance to the harbour.
What navigation is there ?

Both sailing vessels and quite a large number of steamers. The navigation on Lake Winnipeg is getting to be quite important.
Lake Dauphin-lowering lake by removing obstructions from bed of Mossy river, $7,000.
What is the nature of that ?
This is a revote towards the construction and equipment and installation of the plant required for removing these obstructions. It is expected to carry on the work during the present year.
How much has been spent there ?
Nothing has been expended yet.
Does the government intend building a plant and doing the work itself, or is it to be by contract ?
The government will do the work itself.
Who is going to do the work at Grand Marais Harbour ?

We have not decided yet.
Winnipegosis lake-dredging channel at mouth of Mossy river, $5,000.
This work will be done by the government dredge.
Where is that dredge working at the present time ?
The dredge has been removed two or three times since the spring opened. I am not able to tell my hon. friend where it is working just at the moment.

I notice once more that there is no appropriation in the main estimates for the completion of the work that was begun on' the harbour of St. Laurent on Lake Manitoba. Previous to the last election a wharf was built there and a dredge was sent up and for a time there was great activity ; but the moment the election was over, the work ceased, the dredge was taken away, and nothing has been done since. The work that has been done is of utterly no value to the district until it is completed. The council of the municipality has sent a petition asking the government to make the necessary appropriation to complete the work. If the minister has not that petition, I have a copy of it. I have brought this matter up at every session of this parliament, and I have always been stood off with the promise that an item would be brought down in the supplementary estimates, but that has never been done. The work, if completed, would be of great value to the people of that district. They could send wood and other products by boat to Winnipeg, but boats cannot get to the wharf until some further dredging is done. There will also have to be a road made to the wharf. At present produce cannot be taken to or away from the wharf. I would ask the minister if it is his intention to make any provision in the supplementary estimates for the completion of that work.
Is Lake Manitoba in the hon. gentleman's constituency ?
Yes, in the northern part.

I had some information that the work was not regarded as very necessary, because there was not a very large population there. I may have been mininformed as to that, and I will look very carefully into the matter.

It must be of some importance when the reeve and council went to the trouble of drafting a petition and sending it down here. It is of the utmost importance to the people of that district. I think I know the riding and what is required there as well as the people who may have advised the minister. There is another place up there-Delta and Lake Manitoba. Is anything being done there?

There has been some dredging done at the Delta. If further dredging is required, it will be done, but I cannot say just now what will be done.
Old Man's river-diversion of stream into its original bed at McLeod '(revote) $8,000.
Has the minister any information with reference to the damage done by the recent flood? I asked him that question the other evening.
I inquired in my department and find that we have no breakwater there.
There was an appropriation of $8,000 for the work
There was, but nothing is done, and we are now revoting that amount.
Do the government propose spending sufficient money to protect the banks at that point?
The intention of the department is to make the work complete. If it should cost more than $8,000, we shall do what is necessary.

It is very important that some protection should be given.
New dredging plant-maritime provinces,
Are you building new dredges for the maritime provinces?
Not as yet, but new dredging plant is very urgently required. This is to build or acquire one or more dredges and some tugs.
You have no plan in view ?

I have discussed the matter with the chief engineer and superintendent of dredging. They think we ought to have at least three additional dredges-one for work in the Bay of Fundy, one for work in the Baie des Chaleurs, and the other on the north shore. Then we want a number of tugs. In the operation of the dredge ' Fielding ' we ought to have four tugs, and have none available. We have to hire tugs.
Is this $100,000 going to build three dredges and four tugs?

No, that will not begin to do it.
Roads and bridges-Shellmouth bridge over Assiniboine river, $20,000.
Will the minister explain what has been done in connection with the Shellmouth bridge ?

That is under contract. The piers have been completed, and work on the steel superstructure is being carried or. as rapidly as possible. The material I think is all on the ground. I hope the bridge will be completed during the present year. The contract was let for the steel work on the 23rd of October, 1907, to be completed a year from date.
There has been a vote in the estimates for the last four years.
Yes, the work was commenced in 1900.
The old bridge has been condemned for the last four years, and the people are much dissatisfied with the slow progress.

It is impossible to expedite the work any more. Our latest information is that the work is proceeding quite satisfactorily, and we expect it will be completed within the time mentioned.
Land and cable telegraph lines, lower St. Lawrence and maritime provinces, including working expenses of vessels required for cable service and. Marconi wireless telegraph system at Belle Isle, &e., $120,000.
How is the Marconi system working ?
I think it is giving pretty good satisfaction. But this is a matter coming within the Marine Department.
Has the minister got a statement of the revenue and expenditure In this connection ?

The hon. gentleman will find that in the Auditor General's Report.
Harbours and rivers-Quebec harbour improvements, $500,000.
Who has the contract there ?
Dussault & Co.
What is the total estimated amount this work is to cost when completed ?

The work that is going on there is of very great importance. If my hon. friend will come over here I will show him the plans. It will give altogether about 3,000 feet frontage.
Port Arthur and Fort William-harbour and river improvements, $500,000.
Mil-. BENNETT. What is going to be done there this year ?

Just the dredging work. We are doing it as rapidly as possible There will be something done probably in the way of building a revetment wall as well. There is also a breakwater being built at Port Arthur. I may say that for several months, ever since I have been at the head of the department, and I think before that, there has been a strong pressure upon the part of business men of Winnipeg and Port Arthur, also of ship owners, and I think of the boards of trades of those cities, to build a new breakwater out further from the wnarf iu order to give more sea room to the large steamers which are now frequenting the port. I have decided to accede to tfie wishes of the people in this respect. The breakwater, when completed, will give more sea room, because further from the existing wharfs. In the meantime we are leaving n portion of the old breakwater and doing some work of a temporary character. The dredging done will give accommodation to the largest steamers on the lake.
Will the cost of the breakwater come out of this vote?
Yes, part of it.
What portion of this vote will go to the breakwater?
When the breakwater is finally completed it will cost a great deal more than this vote. For the present year we expect the breakwater expenditure . to be about $100,000.
How much will the revetment wall cost?

We have not determined upon that yet. I think perhaps we will have to extend that work over a couple or three years as it will be eoo expensive to be all done iu one year. By building Ihe revetment wall as designed by the chief

engineer we shall save large expense tor building the breakwater opposite the entrance to the Mission river.
Is it intended to spend more in these works ?
I think we shall have to make further provision before parliament rises.
That will be in the supplementary estimates?

Yes. Dredging is going on night and day in order to hurry the work. The Grand Trunk Pacific are laying out their works on a large scale and so is the 'Canadian Pacific Railway, and both are eager to be able to effectively handle the grain trade this fall. We are rushing our work, believing that what we are doing will be a great national benefit.
Is the dredging done under contract? And who is the contractor ?	t
Yes. The Great Lakes Dredging Company.

How many dredges
have they employed?
I think five.

Who is the engineer in charge?	~	<
(Mr. PUGSLEY. Mr. Merrick.
Mr.' BENNETT. Is any other dredging being done besides that by the Great Lakes Dredging Company?
At Port Arthur, Mr. Weddell. I think he has about completed his work.
How much of this is tor Mr. Weddell's work?

Only about 30,000 yards remains to be done at 9 cents a yard.
Red Deer-improvements at St. Andrews Rapids, $300,000.
When will this work be completed?
I hope this year. We made arrangements with the contractors to expedite the work. They carried it on all winter. We hope that this season it will be completed.
Who are the contractors?

Messrs. Quinlan & Robertson.
Transportation facilities, Georgian bay to Montreal-survey for waterway via French and Ottawa rivers, including payments authorized notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act. $10,000.
How much has been expended on this survey so far?

According to my notes the total expenditure to 31st March, 1907, was $597,838.48. But the chief engineer tells me that the memo, must be wrong and that the date should be 31st March, 1908. It will require $40,000 more.
It is expected that this vote will entirely complete the work of the survey. The survey is completed and only some verification work is being done.
What is the intention of the government as to going on with this work ?

My hon. friend will understand that it is a matter of great importance and of great interest to the country, one which will involve the expenditure of a very large sum of money. It is one, therefore, which the government will have to consider after having carefully studied the report submitted. In due course and in proper season the Prime Minister will, no doubt, announce the policy of the government.
Has it been considered by the government?

Not since the report came in.
Port Colborne-harbour improvements, $20,000.
What has the elevator there cost to date?
It is being built by the Department of Railways and Canals, so I cannot give the information. We are building the breakwater.
How much has the Department of Public Works spent there?
The total expenditure of my department is in the vicinity of $850,000, probably pretty close to $900,000.
Has the minister any idea of what the Department of Railways has spent there?
I cannot tell.
I guess you have made it four millions there.
Is this vote for no other purpose than breakwaters?
No.
Who has the contract for the breakwater?
Hogan has one contract and Hogan & Macdonald have another.
Is the minister aware whether the elevator is finished or not?
I do not know.

It was stated in the newspapers some time ago that it is all



1214(8
finished. It does not matter much in any case. It will never do anything.
Militia Department-pay and allowances. $1,500,000.
I suggest that item 71 he allowed to stand as I wish to make a statement upon it which will take some time and other members will probably wish to speak upon it.
I am quite sure that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) will want to discuss several items, but 'he is not present and will wish to be present when the minister makes his statement.	*

That is one reason I did not wish to make it to-night. 'It will be understood that any militia item may be discussed on the item we are leaving, No. 71. Item No. 72, pay and allowances, is for the permanent force. The full vote is $1,500,000. The total number of the permanent force at present is about 3,000.
What is the increase of

There'has been an increase of about 300 in the force since last year.
Salaries and wages, $85,000.
There Is an increase of $15,000.
Last year $15,000 was included in the supplementary estimates.

I would ask the minister if he has seen the following item in the Toronto ' Globe ?'
If there is any part of the provincial expenditure upon which the pruning-knife can properly be used, it is the militia estimates. We are not at war, nor likely to become so. We are threatened with bankruptcy-the only way of averting it is to reduce the expenditure-and there are comparatively few items upon which economy can be used, without injury to the public interests. If the whole militia service was suspended for one, two or three years, the injury done to the country would be so infinitesimal as to be unworthy of notice.

I had not seen it, I will look it up. I did not suppose the Toronto ' Globe ' would publish anything so nonsensical as that. Is it an editorial ?
Mr. BENNETx. It is quoted in the Globe' newspaper of July 2nd. It is a reproduction from the 'Globe' of 1858, 50 years ago, but it is strongly ominous, it is a case of history repeating itself and I think the public will think so.
At page Q-52 of the Auditor General's Report I find an item
under Petawawa camp, Savage, W. J., painting $900. Was that work done by tender and were there any other tenders received?

By tender called by public advertisement. In all the work at Petawawa tenders were asked by 'public advertisements in the newspapers.
Militarv properties-construction and repairs, $258,750.

There is an increase of $45,000 there.
!Sir FREDERICK BORDEN. This includes repairs and rifle ranges, barracks and ordnance stores, &c., and these requirements are annually increasing. The number of rifle ranges is increasing each year and the outlay is increasing somewhat.
The permanent force is now about 3,000. How many were there eight or nine years ago ?

About 800 or 900.
%

REID It has increased about fourfold.
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Between three and fourfold. There is an increase for Halifax and Esquimalt alone of 1.500. That is the principal increase.
Repairs to Quebec cliffs and walls, $40,000.
This is done by day labour. It is the usual, vote.

I trust the minister will put in an appropriation to enable him to repair the military buildings at Kingston. There is a good deal of money spent at Quebec in one way and another, but the Kingston fortifications are allowed to go to ruin. A few years ago a comparatively small expenditure would have put the military property there in good shape.

That is a matter which must be taken up very soon unless we are to allow the whole of that property to go. I found it out of repair and almost abandoned when I came to office. An unsuccessful attempt was made by General Herbert to utilize some of the rooms at Fort Henry. I have had an examination made by engineers within the last year, but I have not yet had an opportunity of looking into the report. I think there will be some small items in the supplementary estimates for some of the works at Kingston to which my hon. friend refers, particularly for the wail bordering the military property,

I would like to know whether the lowest tender was accepted for the painting of these buildings to which I have referred. I understand that several firms in the town of Pembroke tendered, but the Kingston firm got the contract.

I am quite sure the lowest tender was accepted, but I will have the matter looked up.
Warlike and other stores, $350,000.
This is the usual vote.
There is an increase of $37,000. What does this include?
Accoutrements, camp equipment, general stores, engineer's stores and medical stores.
What is meant by the upkeep of armament?

Ammunition both for practice and reserve supply, field and garrison artillery, ordnance stores, transport vehicles, extra parts of outfit for big guns, &c.; artillery stores of which there is a great variety.
In these different items for the militia department there is an increase in the total vote of about $342,000.
And then there are the supplementaries.
There will be no supplementaries except for the militia annual drill.

This vote for clothing and necessaries in stores amounts altogether to $800,000 and that seems a very large amount to expend in one year. One would think that the stores and clothing would not have to go on increasing year after year. Why is there this increase?

The increase in the number of the militia is the principal reason. New corps are being formed in the new provinces of the west to take the place largely of the Northwest Mounted Police. I have a comparative statement here which may be interesting:
