The very great increase of the growth of the militia between the two periods will account ifor a considerable increased portion of the increased cost. The men must have clothing, arms, and ammunition.
How often is new clothing issued?

Once in three years. There is an attempt being made to be more economical, and I think the overcoats are now issued for nine years.
. Mr. DANIEL. You do not issue boots?

Not except to the permanent force.
386i
'Mr. J. D. REID. $300,000 a year for elothing seems a large amount.

It is only an average of about $6 per year for each man.
Provisions and supplies, $430,000.
Why the increase in this vote?
That is principally for the permanent force.
I have seen complaints that the goods furnished have not been up to standard in some cases.
These supplies for the permanent force are purchased by tenders called for in the newspapers.
Open to everybody?

Open to everybody. As to complaints, there was a complant from Halifax by a man who did not get the contract, as his tender was not low enough. He was very much annoyed because the bacon was brought somewhere from Ontario, and endeavoured to make all the trouble he could. As a matter of fact, the food is inspected every day, and every soldier has an opportunity to make a complaint if he chooses. There is absolutely nothing in that story.

I have heard of other cases ; but in that particular case I understand that it was rolled bacon that was supplied. I am not in the militia, but I understand that if a militiaman were to make a complaint to the officer in charge, he would be liable to get into trouble. If the officer in charge stands in with these parties in any way, it would be useless to make a charge to him.

I can assure my hon. friend that we are not running the militia in that way. If I knew that an officer refused to take cognizance of a complaint of that kind, I should dismiss him at once. Our object is to get the very best food we can, and we always accept the lowest tender. Sometimes, when there is keen competition, and a man is foolish enough to tender below the value of the goods supplied, there may be an attempt to skimp, and deliver food which is not up to the mark ; but our inspectors will detect and punish such conduct at once.
Has the supply officer any control over the purchase of goods ?

Not over the purchasing. That is all done by tender, and is determined by the director of contracts here. But the supply officer has absolute control over the quality of the food. That is his business, and he inspects everything that is delivered every morning.

He is not the only one. There is another officer who goes around every morning with the supply officer and the medical officer, so that I do not think there is much chance of inferior food being provided.
If any inferior food should have been delivered, the supply officer has the authority to refuse it and purchase good food and charge it up to the contractor.

If the food is bad, the officer of the day is to blame, because he inspects it at six o'clock in the morning, and has a right to report it to the commanding officer. So that I do not see how improper food could be supplied. I would like to ask the minister, did the report that the bacon was bad come from the men?
No, it came from the disappointed contractor.

I do not mean to say that the food supplied was bad food ; but the contract called for rolled bacon, which had been supplied for years before, and the man at Halifax who tendered supposed that he would have to supply rolled bacon. The man who got the contract quoted a lower price than rolled bacon could be supplied for. The result was that rolled bacon was not supplied. I have not seen any statement in any newspaper either by the department at Ottawa or by the officer in command at Halifax, denying the statement that was in the Halifax paper. That convinces me that rolled bacon was not supplied by the contractor. There was no investigation by the department to find out whether the statement in the newspaper was true or not. 1'herefore until I have further evidence, I am perfectly satisfied that the contractor did not carry out the contract, and that the men did not get the quality of food which the government intended to supply them. They were deceived and the government was defrauded so far as that contract was concerned.

My hon. friend reverses the good old rule of holding a man innocent until he is proven guilty. If I were to occupy my time in answering all the false statements that are made in regard to the department and the way it is administered, it would take all my time. I do not propose to do that. We have a regular means, as hon. gentlemen know, by which every complaint from the humblest man in the force can reach me or his superior officer. In this case I did not think that I was called on to make an investigation, ^ because no charge was made except one in an utterly unreliable newspaper, coming from a disappointed contractor.
Was there ever anv charge made by (be commander of that regiment as .to the quality of the food ?
None whatever.

Did the officer of the day for inspecting the rations make any reports ?
Sir, FREDERICK BORDEN. His reports were ail favourable. There has never been any question or challenge of this particular article. My hon. friend says there has been no contradiction. I have no doubt whatever that the bacon which was tendered for was delivered.
Grants to rifle and artillery associations and bands, $55,000.
What is the basis upon wiiich these grants are made ? Does every rifle company get a grant ?

The basis is $1 per head up to forty and fifty cents for every additional member up to eighty, so that $60 would be the maximum. This is for civilian rifle associations.
Royal Military College, $95,000.
There are slight increases in the professors' salaries and the general expenses are greater.
What salaries are increased ?
The adjutant of the college gets an increase of $500 ; the professor of mathematics $300.
Is this a special increase for the adjutant ?
It will be paid to his successor. It is for the adjutant of the college.
I see the caterer has resigned. What system is now followed ? The system in vogue should be condemned.

The caterer used to receive 50 cents a head. He wanted GO cents. I thought that was rather a large increase and sent an officer to investigate.
I am satisfied we can do very much better by taking charge of the food ourselves within the college as at the different depots. The officers are anxious for the change.
I have heard various yarns about the officers being surprised at the stuff the boys had to eat.
So I believe.
There are several military officers there, are they entitled to rations ? Are any of these rations turned over to the caterer
That has never been done.
Is this vote of $95,000 over and above any fees received ?

We get the
fees back and that reduces the cost very considerably.

With reference to this case at Halifax which the minister said was an impossible one, I have heard other men in charge of different companies out at drill complain about the food served at the camps. They are afraid, however, to kick, because these goods were supplied by f riends of the government and they would get into trouble tnemselves. I have heard those stories and believe them to be true. In a case like that at Halifax, although the minister states that the paper which published it is not reliable,
I think that he or some of his officers would not have been doing any too much if they had at once written to the man. in charge of the regiment and found out what truth there was in the statement, if any. The minister and his deputy did not do their duty when they paid no attention to that. A matter of that kind affecting all those men is a very serious matter. We shall not have time this session to find out the truth in the Fublic Accounts but we will next session. But outside of that case altogether, there are other cases ; and I am perfectly satisfied that the minister would, if he would state what he knows to be true, tell us that he has had complaints of the food furnished the men in the camps at different places.

If any of these complaints are justifiable and if T were in the minister's place, the head would go off every officer in the force who had anything to do with inspecting the rations.. Perhaps the hon. member does not know the routine. I have seen where quartermasters would stand in with the supply oflicers ; but in addition to the quartermasters, there is the field officer of the day, who has the rank of colonel or major, who has to inspect the rations every morning. Then for every regiment there is a regimental officer, and for every company, a company officer, so that the "food has to go through a series of inspections. Besides there is the field medical officer and also the regimental medical officer Unless the officers are absolutely crooked or stupid, it is impossible that stuff not fit to eat could reach the men. If the hon. member had ever been in camp, he would know that the soldiers would kick in a second if they did not get good rations. That is the reason why. when I read this thing about Halifax, I thought the officers and men must be insane to pass such rations. or else they did not know the quality of the goods. The medical officer should detect anything of that kind in a moment. I was going to speak of the Royal Military College. I give the minister notice that at another sitting I intend to discuss the commandant of that college and the system of
discipline pursued there, what they used to term the commission of inquiry into conduct, but what I call the sweat-box system. It is no way to train young men to be manly and straightforward. So far as I am concerned, my vote will go against any man who maintains such a system and against the voting of any money to maintain it.

In following what the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Sam. Hughes) has said, I wish to relieve the mind of my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid). What this committee has been told is exactly right-the men will not stand bad rations. I have had a great deal of experience in camp in the last forty years, both under this administration and under former administrations. As a rule, the rations were good. I can recall one instance several years ago when sour bread was furnished.

Yes, under Conservative administration. The men had no fear of the contractor. They formed a line of three or four hundred feet long, and the bakers' apprentices who brought the bread had to run the gauntlet, the men pelting them with the bread. The next day the bread supplied was sweet. The food goes through a series of inspection, and there is very little danger that the men do not receive what is being paid for and what they are entitled to get.
Dominion Arsenal, $350,000.
Where is that?
At Quebec.
Why the increase?
That is not really an increase. In other years there has been a vote in the supplementary estimates, but this year there will be none.

I ought to know, but I fear I do not. Is it the intention to continue the manufacture of the cartridge 303 as made to-day, or to adopt a modern cartridge, the sharp-pointed bullet? The United States have adopted this form, and the British government will probably adopt It, too, before the end of the century. The Canadian government should be in line and adopt the new pointed bullet. It has much greater initial velocity, lower trajectory and less windage. It is capable of much greater accuracy in firing.
I have not lost sight of the subject. We have the report of an officer who has been in England and investigated the matter.
Did he make inquiry as to what has been done in England by private parties? Private companies in England have adopted this bullet.
This officer has seen the manufacturers there.
I would recommend him to look into what the American manufacturers are doing. If he looks into the matter, he will find in the United States a record that will surprise him.

I desire to call attention to a statement that was made in the public press, that at a recent camp at Niagara it was found out, just in time, that a lot of ammunition supposed to be blank was found to be loaded with slugs, and that the discovery was made just in time to prevent serious casualties.

The report in the newspapers was contradicted by General Cotton at once. There is no truth in it. As usual, before going into the sham fight, all the men were searched for cartridges of every kind, and these few were found. They would have been found in any case. They were in possession of the men for target firing. They were improperly kept, no doubt.
But I suppose there are no such cartridges manufactured, those loaded with slugs?
We are bringing in a great deal of stuff from England, large orders of guns, and everything that comes from the outside is charged duty. That comes out of our pockets and goes into the customs.
Could not the minister reconsider this regulation and allow officers' uniforms to come in free of duty? Officers purchasing uniforms in England have to pay duty.

I am afraid we cannot treat officers differently from others. The only thing that can be done is to buy our uniforms in Canada. I stated in this House a year ago that I could see no reason why officers should not get their clothing made in Canada. I think that is the proper thing to do, and I do not believe it would cost them as much as it does in England.

I have always maintained for the last forty years that the officers should get an aliowaince, that they should be furnished a certain amount for their uniform. As soon as an officer is qualified he should get a certain amount for the purchase of a proper uniform.
No.
How much is it estimated will be paid to the Ross Rifle Company for rifles out of the estimates this year?
The item out of which the rifles will be paid for is the one reserved. The price is $25, and the annual number to be delivered under the contract is 10,000.
That means a maximum payment of $25,000.
You cannot tell exactly. A certain amount is paid as advance and a certain amount of the last instalment on the finished gun.

When we reach tin item perhaps the minister could have statement showing the estimate of wb; will be paid to the Ross Rifle Compar during the year.
Civil government-Department of Labour-salaries, $21,750; contingencies, $1,450.

Under this item I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Labour to some matters in connection with the importation of foreign labour from the United States and other foreign countries. It is said, and I believe with truth, that the working of our Alien Labour law is by no means satisfactory. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent, anil in every other riding where there is a coast line, the same difficulty has been found to exist, namely, that the administration of our present Alien Labour law is very lax indeed: it lacks that rigidity and that honesty of enforcement which will alone carry out the letter as well as the spirit of the Act. With regard to the condition of things in the riding of Sault Ste. Marie, I can best illustrate it by reading a copy of a petition which is now, I believe, in the hands of the minister:

Yes if they are delivered.
Customs dues. $200,000.
Why such a great increase in this item?
are on the other side of the border. I feel sure that the minister will approach the consideration of the matter in that sense of fairness which characterizes his treatment of such questions.

I thank my hon. friend for bringing this matter up this evening. His remarks as they appear in ' Hansard' will serve me to morrow as a brief for the Minister of Justice. It is true that practically the administration of the labour law is in the hands of the (Minister of Labour, but when these cases are taken to the At-' torney General of Canada, that is the Minister of Justice, he acts jointly with me. My hon. friend says we should have a law similar in its effects to the law in the neighbouring republic. I believe in retaliatory measures, we should favour the doctrine of an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. The Alien Labour law, we must all admit was less workable a few years ago than it appears to be to-day. Some years ago, as my hon. friend knows from his professional experience, the only remedy that the parties had was to address themselves to the Attorney General for Canada, the Minister of Justice, and obtain Ms good pleasure for the fiat. Since then, under the administration of the Department of Labour by Sir William Mulock, and of the Justice Department by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, the present Chief Justice of Canada, the law has been so amended as to give the parties the right to obtain a fiat from the Attorney General of each province or from a judge of the Superior Court or a county court judge. The penalty also has been modified in degree. Some years ago the only penalty which could be imposed was a fine of $1,000, and in the application of the law, as the penalty was so severe and the law by its nature so drastic, the judges were inclined to be conservative in its application and in 99 cases out of 100 would give the benefit of the doubt to the defendant. An amendment to the law has been adopted by which the judges are at liberty to impose a penalty ranging from $50 to $1,000.
I admit with my hon. friend that we might go a step farther and make the penalty more severe in this sense, that if the penalty is not paid and if the deportation does not take place we might be more drastic and severe. However, as this is something of an international character, for in fact our law applies only to the United States and such United States possessions as are near our boundary, I will not say what other more drastic penalty we will impose, but my hon. friend can surmise what it Is. I know that from his district the department has been notified on two occasions, first by the Sault Ste. Marie labour element and then by the Port Arthur people, of trouble under the existing law. We received a message in April, I think, from the mayor of Port Arthur complaining that labourers were imported from Duluth whilst there Mr. BOYCE.
were plenty of people in Port Arthur to do the work. We immediately put ourselves into communication with the parties and since then the matter has been dropped. At all events the department will be always disposed to help those who will invoke the law. I may say it has not been a dead letter on the statute-book. If my hon. friend will read the report of the Department of Labour for this year he will find a series of cases reported there. This Alien Labour law, as he stated a moment ago, being retaliatory in its nature, has been subjected to many checks by the courts. For instance we all remember the famous judgment of Mr. Justice Anglin. During the period between the judgment of Mr. Justice Anglin and the final judgment of the Privy Council reversing his decision, nearly all cases were stopped. However, since that time the law has been applied and judgments have been rendered which show the law is not ineffective and has been applied in many instances. I have no doubt the remarks of my hon. friend which have been made in a fair spirit will have weight.
I shall communicate with the Minister of Justice and see what better provision can be made to render the law more pliable and .more effective in protecting our own people against the alien labour.

It will be noticed that there are a few decreases which are largely due to readjustments of the offices, as where an old officer passes away and in the 1 earrangement of the office the expense is somewhat less. The only item of increase of any importance is in regard to the expense of printing Dominion notes, -that will probably increase every year with the increased volume of business and with the desire that has been expressed by members on both sides for cleaner currency.
Superintendent of Insurance, to meet expenses in connection with this service, $23,450.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The salary of the superintendent is fixed by statute and we are proposing a resolution concerning it. This is for the ordinary expense of the department which is enlarging all the time in a small degree.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.

I wish to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance to

an article which appeared in the papers to-day, which reads- as follows :
Pierson, Manitoba, July 6.-A horde of religious fanatics struck town on Saturday. They were all armed with Winchester rifles and revolvers, and knives, and declared they would not abide by the laws of sinful man, and would shoot anybody that interfered with them. The leader of the gang, a grizzly-faced looking veteran, claimed he was 'Jesus Christ/ and that he was going to Yorkton to look after the Doukhobors there, who were wandering without fi leader. They were a very tattered looking outfit, as if they had tramped a long distance, and claimed to have come from Missouri, where they were persecuted by the United States authorities.
Constable Macfarlane, of the Manitoba Mounted Police, who happened to be here, had rather a warm time. On his demanding from them where they were going, and advancing towards them, they pointed their rifles at him, and told him if he made another step they would fire.
After a harangue from the leader, to which the rest joined in with loud ' Amen,' they proceeded west. It was not thought wise to interfere with them.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if this matter has been drawn to the attention of the government, and if they are allowing these people to come into our country from the United States without taking any action?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no information on the subject. Possibly some of my colleagues may have received some information, but I think we might trust matters of that kind to the tender mercies of the Attorney General of Manitoba.

I think these men will be found not to be of the better class of American citizens, but what I call galvanized Yankee anarchists, like the men who were cutting each others' throats a short time ago in the neighbourhood of Medicine Hat. The United States immigrants who come into the country will not be found to be of that type at all.
In a case of that kind does the Dominion government not interfere, but leave it entirely in the hands of the local government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I speak on the general principle that the preservation of law and order is in the hands of the local authorities.
It will be of interest to the House to know that in all probability the Cornwall canal will be open for navigation on Saturday next.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Prime Minister intimated to me early in the evening that it had been arranged that what is called the Hodgins matter would be taken up in the morning, but I have been informed quite recently that some hon. gentlemen who are anxious to discuss that matter had arranged that it would not come on until the afternoon. We may assume that either that or the Civil Service Bill will be taken up in the morning and both during the day, and, if we reach Supply, we will take up the estimates of the Minister of Railways and Canals.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.40 p.m.
Tuesday, July 7, 1908.
